extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, epistemology, and evidential reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria for evaluating testimony, miracles, coincidences, and observations as evidence in inductive reasoning; includes how to judge improbability, counteracting causes, and when to suspend judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracle evidence and antecedent improbability
rubrics_metrics.description: “A miracle ... is a new effect, supposed to be produced by the introduction of a new cause. Of the adequacy of that cause, if present, there can be no doubt; and the only antecedent improbability which can be ascribed to the miracle, is the improbability that any such cause existed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No amount of testimony can prove a miracle to someone who does not already believe in beings with supernatural power, because there is always the alternative hypothesis of some unknown natural cause; to admit a miracle requires extraordinary antecedent probability from the special circumstances to outweigh the antecedent improbability that such a supernatural cause existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: General presumption against special divine interposition
rubrics_metrics.description: “...religion, following in the wake of science, has been compelled to acknowledge the government of the universe as being on the whole carried on by general laws... there is a general presumption against any supposition of divine agency not operating through general laws.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Belief that the universe is governed by general laws creates an antecedent improbability for any hypothesis of special divine intervention; such a presumption must be overcome by very strong evidence in particular cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict with ascertained laws of causation
rubrics_metrics.description: “The assertion that a cause has been defeated of an effect which is connected with it by a completely ascertained law of causation, is to be disbelieved or not, according to the probability or improbability that there existed in the particular instance an adequate counteracting cause.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To judge such assertions estimate the likelihood that a known counteracting cause was present at the time and place in question, using previous knowledge of the frequency or rarity of such causes rather than conjecture about their general existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating antecedent improbability by frequency at time/place
rubrics_metrics.description: “…we are seldom, therefore, without the means (when the circumstances of the case are at all known to us) of judging how far it is likely that such a cause should have existed at that time and place…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment focuses on the probability that a counteracting cause was present in the specific instance (time and place), drawing on known frequencies or rarity of known causes; we are not required to judge their general existence in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of alleged new Kinds (disconformable in specie)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an alleged fact conflicts with uniformities of mere co-existence (properties of Kinds), the fact asserted is the existence of a new Kind; which in itself is not in the slightest degree incredible, and only to be rejected if the improbability that any variety existing at that place/time should not have been discovered sooner, be greater than that of error or mendacity in witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assertions of new kinds from unexplored places by credible observers are not automatically disbelieved but regarded as requiring confirmation from subsequent observers unless the alleged properties contradict known properties of a larger Kind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of incredibility tied to generality of violated uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: “When the generalization is very comprehensive, embracing a vast number and variety of observations... then... any alleged exception to it can not be admitted, unless on the evidence of some law of causation proved by a still more complete induction.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions to very general empirical laws approach the certainty of ascertained causal laws and thus demand correspondingly stronger evidence (possibly evidence sufficient to establish a new law of causation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute impossibility limited to most general laws
rubrics_metrics.description: “Those which are true of all things whatever, or at least which are totally independent of the varieties of Kinds, namely, the laws of number and extension, to which we may add the law of causation itself, are probably the only ones, an exception to which is absolutely and permanently incredible.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that violate the most general laws (e.g., arithmetic, extension, causation) are treated as absolutely and permanently impossible; violations of more specialized laws are judged as improbable but not absolutely impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension of judgment when testimony lacks suspicious circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: “...a cautious person will neither admit nor reject the testimony, but will wait for confirmation at other times and from other unconnected sources.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an alleged anomaly does not contradict universal or near-universal laws and the testimony, when sifted, presents no suspicious circumstances, the prudent response is to suspend judgment and seek independent confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstances that render testimony untrustworthy
rubrics_metrics.description: “…there have almost always been circumstances which, to a keen observer who had taken due pains to sift the matter, would have rendered the testimony untrustworthy. There have generally been means of accounting for the impression... by fallacious appearances; or some epidemic delusion...; or some strong interest...—religious zeal, party feeling, vanity, or at least the passion for the marvelous…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating testimony look for fallacious sensory appearances, collective delusions, or vested interests (religious zeal, party feeling, vanity, love of the marvelous) that could explain error or mendacity; their presence lowers the credibility of testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between improbability before and after the fact
rubrics_metrics.description: The mistake of overlooking the distinction between 'improbability before the fact and improbability after it'; many events improbable beforehand are not incredible after being asserted because they are not contrary to known inductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reject an asserted fact merely because it was improbable a priori; if the fact is one of a class where some equally improbable outcome must have occurred (e.g., a particular die throw or a particular death-date), credible testimony can justify belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of coincidences and motive-to-falsehood effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Coincidences (peculiar combinations of chances) are often regarded as more improbable and as requiring stronger evidence, because they 'excite wonder' and thus increase motives to falsehood or exaggeration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a reported coincidence is remarkable, consider that it may be more likely to be falsely asserted (desire to astonish); but also consider cases where witnesses, impressed by extraordinariness, may be more careful. Each case must be evaluated on its particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-principles evaluation of coincidences (Laplace critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: “To know whether a coincidence does or does not require more evidence to render it credible than an ordinary event, we must refer, in every instance, to first principles, and estimate afresh what is the probability that the given testimony would have been delivered in that instance, supposing the fact which it asserts not to be true.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply blanket rules (e.g., Laplace’s generalization) to all coincidences; analyze the structure of possible errors/mendacity in each instance (how many alternative errors exist, witness knowledge/biases) and compute how likely the testimony would arise if false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation must be distinguished from inference
rubrics_metrics.description: “The sole condition is, that what is supposed to have been observed shall really have been observed; that it be an observation, not an inference.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relying on reported observations, verify that the report concerns direct sensation (what the observer actually perceived) rather than inferences drawn from sensations (e.g., identifying a voice or person). Many so-called errors of sense are erroneous inferences from genuine sensations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensations vs. judgments: source of 'errors of sense'
rubrics_metrics.description: “All, however, which is really perception, is that I hear a sound. That the sound is a voice ... are not perceptions but inferences... There are none of them properly errors of sense; they are erroneous inferences from sense.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that perceptual reports include both sensory data and interpretive judgment; errors often arise in the interpretive layer (misidentification, hallucination, deceptive contexts such as kaleidoscope or dreams), so evaluating observation reliability requires parsing these components.
